triage.name: Central retinal vein occlusion
triage.reason: Sudden painless vision loss with diffuse retinal hemorrhages; reachable from vascular risk history, fundoscopy and workup.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: term 'Temporal artery tenderness' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Slightly more common in men in some series
More common in people of African or Hispanic ancestry, largely reflecting higher rates of hypertension and diabetes

chief_complaints.text: My vision went blurry in one eye
Everything looks dark and cloudy in that eye
I can't see well out of the corner of my eye

hpi.onset: Sudden, over minutes to hours, and painless
hpi.duration: Present for hours to a few days at presentation
hpi.progression: Vision loss is usually worst at onset and then stable; a minority worsen over days to weeks as macular edema or new vessels develop
hpi.location: One eye only, usually the whole field
hpi.quality: Blurring, cloudiness, darkening or a curtain over the vision; the eye itself is not painful
hpi.severity: Mild blurring to near-complete loss of vision in the affected eye
hpi.timing: Constant, present on waking or noticed at once

associated_symptoms.text: Visual field defect or loss of peripheral vision
Mild eye ache or pressure sensation

pertinent_negatives: Curtain or shade descending over the vision
Headache with jaw claudication or scalp tenderness
Recent eye trauma or eye surgery

positives.text: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye

argues_against: Flashing lights with a curtain across vision
Focal neurologic deficit suggesting stroke or transient ischemic attack

atypical.how_it_differs: Rare; usually associated with an underlying thrombophilia, dehydration or systemic illness, and the child may not report vision loss clearly.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of sudden monocular vision loss

atypical.how_it_differs: May be attributed to cataract or macular degeneration, and giant cell arteritis must be excluded when presentation is atypical.
Rare; may occur with preeclampsia or a hypercoagulable state, and can be bilateral.
Diabetic retinopathy can mask or coexist with the occlusion, making the fundus picture harder to interpret.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; vision blurring in one eye only
general.moderate: Mildly distressed by monocular visual loss but systemically well
general.severe: Visibly anxious about marked visual loss; otherwise well-appearing
general.critical: Rarely systemically ill; consider another cause if toxic-appearing

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye separately with a Snellen chart or pinhole
findings.finding: Reduced visual acuity in the affected eye, ranging from mild blurring to counting fingers or worse

findings.maneuver: Swing a light between the two eyes and compare the pupillary response
findings.finding: Relative afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Confrontation visual fields in each eye
findings.finding: Visual field defect in the affected eye, often peripheral or altitudinal

findings.maneuver: Dilate the pupil and examine the fundus with direct ophthalmoscopy
findings.finding: Diffuse flame-shaped and dot-blot retinal hemorrhages in all four quadrants

findings.maneuver: Examine the optic disc with direct ophthalmoscopy
findings.finding: Swollen, hyperemic optic disc with blurred margins

findings.maneuver: Examine the retinal vessels with direct ophthalmoscopy
Examine the fundus for white patches
findings.finding: Cotton-wool spots along the vascular arcades

findings.maneuver: Examine the macula with direct ophthalmoscopy or optical coherence tomography
Ask about and assess for ocular pain
Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in room light
Screen cranial nerves, strength, sensation and speech
Palpate the temporal arteries and scalp
findings.finding: No temporal artery tenderness or thickened, nodular temporal arteries

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to chew vigorously and report jaw pain
Measure temperature and ask about fevers

labs.caveat: Fasting glucose; hyperglycemia is a major modifiable risk factor and may be undiagnosed at presentation.
Identifies undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes, which is common in this population.
Hyperlipidemia is a modifiable vascular risk factor.
Chronic kidney disease is a vascular risk factor and affects choice of antihypertensive therapy.
Order when giant cell arteritis is a consideration; a normal ESR and CRP make it much less likely.
Supports giant cell arteritis when elevated; normal values argue against it.
Thrombocytosis or a myeloproliferative neoplasm can predispose to venous occlusion.
Anemia or polycythemia may point to an underlying hematologic disorder.
Prolonged when a hypercoagulable state or liver disease is present.
Consider a thrombophilia workup in younger patients without classic vascular risk factors.
Thyroid disease can contribute to vascular risk and is worth checking in atypical cases.

imaging.study: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
imaging.preferred_when: All patients with suspected central retinal vein occlusion

findings.text: Macular edema with intraretinal cystoid spaces
Hyperreflective dots or thickening of the inner retinal layers

imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain or ischemic disease is suspected

findings.text: Prolonged arteriovenous transit time with delayed venous filling
Dilated, tortuous retinal veins with leakage
Capillary nonperfusion (ischemic central retinal vein occlusion)
Late leakage from the optic disc and retinal vessels

imaging.preferred_when: When noninvasive assessment of retinal perfusion is preferred

findings.text: Reduced capillary perfusion density in the affected retina

imaging.preferred_when: When the fundus cannot be visualized (dense vitreous hemorrhage or media opacity)

findings.text: Optic disc swelling and retinal thickening

imaging.study: MRI brain and orbits with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When a central nervous system cause or optic nerve pathology is suspected

findings.text: Usually normal in isolated central retinal vein occlusion
Optic nerve enhancement or orbital mass when an alternative cause is present

initial.why: Screen for diabetes and hyperglycemia, a major risk factor
Identifies undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes
Assess hyperlipidemia as a modifiable vascular risk factor
Evaluate renal function and electrolytes before antihypertensive therapy
Look for anemia, polycythemia or thrombocytosis

initial.test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
initial.why: Documents macular edema and guides anti-VEGF therapy
Screen for giant cell arteritis in older patients
initial.only_if: age over 50 with atypical features or systemic symptoms

initial.why: Supports the assessment for giant cell arteritis

confirmatory.why: Confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes ischemic from nonischemic occlusion when the clinical picture is unclear

supporting.why: Noninvasive assessment of retinal capillary perfusion
Evaluates the posterior segment when the fundus cannot be seen
supporting.only_if: media opacity or dense vitreous hemorrhage prevents fundoscopy

supporting.why: Thyroid disease can contribute to vascular risk in atypical cases
Thrombophilia workup in younger patients without classic risk factors
Assesses coagulation status when a hypercoagulable state is suspected

not_indicated.test: MRI brain and orbits with and without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for isolated central retinal vein occlusion; reserve for suspected central nervous system or optic nerve disease
No role in the evaluation of retinal vein occlusion
Not indicated unless acute coronary syndrome is suspected
Routine urinalysis does not change management

decision_points: Check for giant cell arteritis in patients over 50 with atypical features; start high-dose corticosteroids immediately if suspected and do not wait for biopsy results
Distinguish ischemic from nonischemic central retinal vein occlusion because ischemic disease carries a high risk of neovascular glaucoma and requires closer follow-up
Control blood pressure, glucose and lipids to reduce the risk of the fellow eye and cardiovascular events
Refer urgently to ophthalmology for anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal corticosteroids when macular edema threatens vision

differential.name: Branch retinal vein occlusion
differential.why_considered: Same risk profile and same sudden painless monocular visual loss from a retinal vein occlusion.

history: Vision loss may be sectoral or milder, sometimes only a field defect
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally
exam: Hemorrhages confined to one sector or quadrant rather than all four quadrants
Optic disc usually not swollen
Visual field defect respects a sector rather than the whole field
imaging: Fluorescein angiography shows delayed venous filling limited to the affected sector
OCT shows macular edema only when the macula is involved

differential.name: Diabetic retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and macular edema in a patient with vascular risk factors.

history: Known diabetes, often long-standing
Gradual rather than sudden visual decline
Bilateral and symmetric involvement
exam: Microaneurysms, hard exudates and dot-blot hemorrhages rather than diffuse flame hemorrhages in all quadrants
Neovascularization at the disc or elsewhere in proliferative disease
No dilated tortuous veins with disc edema
imaging: Fluorescein angiography shows microaneurysms and capillary nonperfusion without delayed venous filling

differential.name: Hypertensive retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and disc edema in a patient with high blood pressure.

history: Known or severely elevated blood pressure
Usually bilateral and gradual
May be asymptomatic
exam: Arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking and copper or silver wiring
Hemorrhages and exudates without the diffuse dilated tortuous veins of a vein occlusion
Bilateral symmetric findings
labs: Renal function abnormalities if malignant hypertension

differential.name: Ocular ischemic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular visual loss with retinal findings in an older patient with vascular disease.
differential.trigger: Monocular vision loss with a dull aching eye, mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages and no disc edema in a patient with carotid bruits or amaurosis fugax

history: Amaurosis fugax or prior transient ischemic attacks
Dull orbital ache rather than painless loss
Symptoms worse in bright light
exam: Mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages rather than diffuse flame hemorrhages in all quadrants
No optic disc edema
Carotid bruit
Iris neovascularization or anterior segment ischemia
imaging: Fluorescein angiography shows delayed choroidal filling and prolonged arm-to-retina time

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular visual loss in a patient over 50, which can present as an arteritic occlusion.
differential.trigger: Age over 50 with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, polymyalgia symptoms or elevated ESR/CRP

history: Headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication
Polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms
Systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss and malaise
Visual loss may be preceded by transient visual obscurations
exam: Tender, thickened or nodular temporal arteries
Pale, swollen optic disc
Reduced temporal artery pulse
imaging: Temporal artery biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation
Vascular ultrasound showing a halo sign in the temporal artery

differential.name: Papilledema from raised intracranial pressure
differential.why_considered: Bilateral disc swelling with visual obscurations and field defects.
differential.trigger: Bilateral disc edema with headache, nausea or transient visual obscurations, especially in a younger or obese patient

history: Headache, nausea or vomiting
Transient visual obscurations with postural change
Often bilateral
exam: Bilateral disc edema
Enlarged blind spot
No diffuse retinal hemorrhages in all quadrants
imaging: MRI brain with venography showing raised intracranial pressure or venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture with elevated opening pressure

differential.name: Vitreous hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular visual loss with floaters and reduced red reflex.

history: Sudden onset of floaters or a red haze
Often associated with trauma, diabetes or retinal tear
exam: Reduced or absent red reflex
Blood in the vitreous obscuring the fundus
No diffuse retinal hemorrhages visible unless the view is clear
imaging: B-scan ultrasound shows vitreous hemorrhage and may show a retinal tear or detachment

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular visual loss with a curtain or shade over the vision.
differential.trigger: Flashes of light followed by a curtain or shade descending over the vision

history: Flashes of light followed by floaters
Curtain or shade descending over the vision
Progressive rather than stable visual loss
exam: Visual field defect corresponding to the detached retina
Elevated retina on fundoscopy
No diffuse retinal hemorrhages
imaging: B-scan ultrasound shows a retinal detachment when the fundus cannot be seen

differential.name: Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular visual loss with disc edema in an older patient with vascular risk factors.

history: Sudden painless visual loss, often noticed on waking
No floaters or field defect typical of retinal disease
exam: Sectoral or diffuse disc edema with a pale disc
Relative afferent pupillary defect
No diffuse retinal hemorrhages or dilated tortuous veins
labs: ESR and CRP to exclude giant cell arteritis

severity.mild: Nonischemic central retinal vein occlusion with mild visual blurring, visual acuity better than 20/40, minimal macular edema and no perfusion defect.
severity.moderate: Nonischemic occlusion with visual acuity 20/40 to 20/200, macular edema on OCT and a visual field defect but no anterior segment neovascularization.
severity.severe: Ischemic central retinal vein occlusion with visual acuity worse than 20/200, extensive capillary nonperfusion on fluorescein angiography and high risk of neovascular complications.
severity.critical: Not applicable; central retinal vein occlusion is not life-threatening, but it can be a marker of significant cardiovascular risk.

red_flags.meaning: Neovascular glaucoma is developing; needs urgent ophthalmology referral and pressure-lowering therapy

red_flags.finding: Severe eye pain with a red eye and decreased vision
red_flags.meaning: Neovascular glaucoma with elevated intraocular pressure; sight-threatening emergency

red_flags.finding: Visual acuity worse than 20/200 or extensive capillary nonperfusion on fluorescein angiography
red_flags.meaning: Ischemic central retinal vein occlusion with high risk of neovascular complications; requires close follow-up

red_flags.finding: Headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness in a patient over 50
red_flags.meaning: Giant cell arteritis; start high-dose corticosteroids immediately and do not wait for biopsy

red_flags.finding: Bilateral involvement or recurrent thrombosis in a young patient
red_flags.meaning: Underlying thrombophilia or systemic disease; needs hematologic workup

complications.name: Macular edema
clues: Progressive blurring or distortion of central vision

complications.name: Neovascular glaucoma
clues: Iris or angle neovascularization on slit lamp
Severe eye pain, red eye and decreased vision

complications.name: Vitreous hemorrhage
clues: Sudden new floaters or red haze
Blood in the vitreous on examination

complications.name: Tractional retinal detachment
clues: Elevated retina on fundoscopy or B-scan ultrasound

complications.name: Optic atrophy
clues: Pale optic disc on follow-up examination

special_populations.differences: Higher risk of ischemic central retinal vein occlusion and neovascular glaucoma; giant cell arteritis must be excluded when presentation is atypical.
Diabetic retinopathy can coexist and mask the occlusion; glycemic control is important and the fundus picture may be harder to interpret.
Rare; may occur with preeclampsia or a hypercoagulable state and can be bilateral; management must consider fetal safety.
Very rare; usually associated with an underlying thrombophilia, dehydration or systemic illness, and the child may not report vision loss clearly.

key_questions.question: When did the vision change start, and was it sudden or gradual?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over minutes to hours, painless, in one eye

key_questions.question: Is the vision loss in one eye or both?
key_questions.looking_for: One eye only; bilateral suggests another cause such as papilledema or giant cell arteritis

key_questions.question: Does the eye hurt, or is it red or tearing?
key_questions.looking_for: No pain, no redness; pain or redness suggests a different diagnosis such as acute glaucoma or uveitis

key_questions.question: Is the whole field affected, or just part of it?
key_questions.looking_for: Diffuse or whole-field blurring and darkening; a sector defect suggests branch vein occlusion

key_questions.question: Do you see flashing lights or a curtain or shade coming down over the vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; flashes followed by a curtain suggest retinal detachment

key_questions.question: Do you see new floaters or a red haze?
key_questions.looking_for: Floaters may occur; a red haze suggests vitreous hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Do things look distorted or wavy?
Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or glaucoma?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia or glaucoma are the main risk factors

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a blood clot, stroke, or a similar problem in the other eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior thrombosis or occlusion suggests a hypercoagulable state or recurrent vascular disease

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including birth control pills or hormone therapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Oral contraceptives, hormone therapy or other agents that raise thrombotic risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and how much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former smoking and heavy alcohol use as modifiable vascular risk factors

key_questions.question: Do you have a headache, scalp tenderness, or pain in your jaw when chewing?
key_questions.looking_for: Present in a patient over 50 suggests giant cell arteritis and needs urgent treatment

key_questions.question: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or double vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; focal neurologic symptoms suggest stroke or another central cause

key_questions.question: Any fever, weight loss, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests systemic illness such as giant cell arteritis or infection

reasoning_points: Sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye in an older adult with vascular risk factors
Fundoscopy shows diffuse flame-shaped and dot-blot hemorrhages in all four quadrants with dilated, tortuous retinal veins and disc edema
No eye pain, redness, flashing lights, or curtain over the vision, which argues against retinal detachment and acute glaucoma
Giant cell arteritis is considered and excluded in patients over 50 with atypical features or systemic symptoms
Optical coherence tomography documents macular edema and guides anti-VEGF therapy
Fluorescein angiography distinguishes ischemic from nonischemic occlusion and assesses the risk of neovascular glaucoma
Blood pressure, glucose, and lipids are evaluated and controlled to reduce the risk of the fellow eye and cardiovascular events

easy: Older adult with hypertension and diabetes
Fundoscopy shows diffuse hemorrhages in all four quadrants with dilated tortuous veins and disc edema
medium: Patient with diabetic retinopathy where the occlusion is harder to see
Mild blurring only, with visual acuity better than 20/40
Branch retinal vein occlusion with sectoral hemorrhages
Older patient where giant cell arteritis must be excluded
hard: Young patient without classic vascular risk factors, raising concern for thrombophilia
Dense vitreous hemorrhage obscuring the fundus so the diagnosis is made on B-scan ultrasound
Presentation with neovascular glaucoma rather than visual loss
Patient with ocular ischemic syndrome from carotid stenosis mimicking the findings
